summary: Even with a median household income north of $212,000 a year, the home-price-to-income ratio here sits above 9:1 — one of the steepest in the entire Bay Area — meaning the gap between earning well and actually buying is a defining feature of daily financial life on the Tiburon peninsula. The setting explains part of the premium: this narrow finger of hilly land juts into the San Francisco Bay, offering unobstructed sightlines to the city skyline, Angel Island, and the Golden Gate Bridge from dozens of residential streets, with Richardson Bay wrapping along the western shore. At just under 9,000 residents spread across 13.3 square miles (much of it open water and protected ridgeline), the density sits around 669 people per square mile — closer to a rural township than a suburb, and the pace reflects it. The compact downtown along Ark Row and Main Street holds a handful of sit-down restaurants, a wine bar or two, and small boutiques, but this is not a place with late-night energy; by 9 p.m. the streets are quiet. The Golden Gate Transit ferry to San Francisco's Financial District takes roughly 25 minutes, making it a textbook bedroom community — almost no major employers anchor the town itself. Average highs hover around 64°F year-round with nearly nine hours of daily sunshine, meaning fog burns off reliably here more than in San Francisco proper. Tiburon is a place where the views are spectacular and the commerce is minimal — a tradeoff baked into the geography itself.
